title: Thinking on Paper: How Writing Strengthens Critical Thinking
author: Matt Hutson
summary: Matt Hutson, an English teacher, uses Howard and Barton's book Thinking on Paper to reflect on why the counterclaim step in argumentative writing often becomes a ceremony performed after the answer is already decided. He separates writing to discover an idea from preparing it for an audience, and proposes three kinds of work on the page: catch the thought, develop it, and test it. Testing means giving an idea a worthy opponent, stating the opposing view so that its holder would recognize it, and being honest about evidence one wants to believe, as in the classic Lord, Ross and Lepper study on biased assimilation. He applies the method to his own claims about five-paragraph essays, a CARE workshop for several teachers, and his wife's advice to spend time on materials rather than another essay. His four outcomes for a tested claim are keep, narrow, investigate further, or replace.
points: The counterargument in school essays often becomes a ritual, so students need time to explore before committing to a thesis.
A useful objection should be stated so the person who holds it recognizes their own reasoning, not rearranged to make your side look larger.
Deliberately considering the opposite works better than telling yourself to be fair, according to the Lord, Lepper and Preston study cited.
Teachers can credit justified revision by assessing how an objection changed a student's claim, its scope or the next question to pursue.
quotes: I have taught argumentative writing for years. I know the familiar sequence: make a claim, support it, address a counterclaim.
The opposing view has appeared on the page without ever having a serious chance to change it.
Discovery gives a thought somewhere to begin. Returning with harder questions gives it a chance to develop.
The problem is, I haven’t truly tested whether my position can hold up against genuine disagreement; I’ve just rearranged the furniture to make my side appear larger.
The weakest response to that concern is that students should follow the format because that is how essays are written.
If a student’s original claim becomes more qualified, I want to assess the reasoning for that change.
Waiting to address every possible criticism might keep the work forever in the notebook.
An idea becomes more useful when I can explain what would make me revise it.
